raw_case_text:
An 85-year-old healthy man presented to the surgery clinic of Ghaem Hospital, complaining of abdominal pain, which was generalized, dull, and acute and started two days before he came to the clinic. The pain was constant, and he declared its intensity 4 out of 10, with no radiation. Moreover, he did not reveal any correlation between pain intensity and eating or activity. He did not mention any recent fever, nausea, or vomiting. He did not report any past medical history of surgery or hospitalization.
On his medical examination, vital signs were as follows: heart rate = 98/min, respiratory rate = 14/min, blood pressure = 115/70 mmHg, and axial temperature = 37.3 C. His abdomen was soft, and there was just a mild generalized tenderness without rebound or guarding. There was no sign of organomegaly, scar, or herniation. The rest of his examination was normal.
Complete blood count was normal, and blood chemistry did not show any abnormal findings other than high ESR (53 mm/hr) and high CRP (187 mg/l) with the normal range of ESR (0-22 mm/hr for men) and CRP < 10 mg/l.
Coronal sections of the abdomen-pelvic CT scan with IV contrast showed a hepatic hydatid cyst with water lily sign in the right lobe of the liver with a compressive effect on the adjacent diaphragm and the left lobe of the liver and hydatid cyst of the bladder dome (Figure 1). In axial sections of the CT scan, hepatic hydatid cysts were seen with water lily sign and pressure effect on the diaphragm and an intact capsule in the right and the left lobes of the liver. Free abdominal fluid was present (Figure 2). In other axial sections of the pelvis, a hydatid cyst was seen with an intact capsule on the bladder dome (Figure 3).
Open abdominal surgery was performed with the final diagnosis of hydatidosis. There was an intact cyst without any invasion right above the bladder with 10*13 cm size and hepatic origin. There was no adhesion, but just a little fibrous tissue was seen between the cyst and bladder.
Further examination of the liver revealed a perforation, and the source of intra-abdominal bloody discharge was from there. Isolated hepatic cysts were aspirated and washed with hypertonic serum. The cysts were not related to the bile ducts, and bile secretions were not seen at the site of the cyst cavity. Pathology samples were sent for further examination. On histopathological examination, hydatid cyst diagnosis was confirmed for the bladder dome cyst (Figure 4).
The postoperative status was good and stable. The patient was discharged four days after the surgery with an albendazole prescription (10 mg/kg, twice a day) and said to visit the surgical clinic next week.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 85-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of acute generalized dull abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The previously healthy octogenarian presented to the surgical clinic with a 2-day history of constant, non-radiating generalized dull abdominal pain (severity 4/10) unrelated to meals or activity.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior surgeries or hospitalizations.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute dull generalized abdominal pain; negative for fever, nausea, or vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: heart rate 98/min, respiratory rate 14/min, blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, and axillary temperature 37.3 C. Abdomen was soft with mild generalized tenderness without rebound tenderness, guarding, organomegaly, scars, or hernia.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and routine serum biochemistry were normal except for an elevated ESR of 53 mm/hr (normal 0-22 mm/hr) and elevated CRP of 187 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L).
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT demonstrated hepatic hydatid cysts in both the right and left hepatic lobes exhibiting the classic water-lily sign and compressing the diaphragm, free intraperitoneal fluid, and a 10 x 13 cm intact cyst overlying the urinary bladder dome. Open exploratory laparotomy identified a perforated hepatic cyst causing bloody intraperitoneal fluid, aspirated and irrigated the hepatic cysts with hypertonic saline, and excised the intact 10 x 13 cm pelvic/bladder-dome cyst; histopathological examination confirmed a hydatid cyst.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Synchronous bilobar hepatic hydatid cysts (with localized hepatic perforation/hemoperitoneum) and a secondary 10 x 13 cm pelvic bladder-dome hydatid cyst, confirmed by the CT water-lily sign and postoperative histopathology. Following open excision of the bladder-dome cyst and aspiration/hypertonic saline washout of the hepatic cysts, the patient was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day 4 on oral albendazole (10 mg/kg twice daily).
